frame: Mo has labelled a poster on the music hut wall. The Whyrella thinks he's wrong.
text: How a Guitar Makes Its Sound. When you pluck a guitar string, it moves backwards and forwards very quickly. This is called vibrating. A thick string vibrates more slowly than a thin one, so it makes a lower note. The vibrating string pushes on the air around it and makes tiny waves. On its own, a string is quite quiet, because it is too thin to move much air. That is why a guitar has a hollow wooden body. The string passes its shaking through the bridge into the thin wooden top of the guitar. The whole top starts to vibrate, and because it is much bigger than the string, it pushes far more air. The air inside the body bounces around and comes out of the round sound hole. By the time the sound reaches your ears, it is many times louder than the string alone. That is why you can hear a guitar from the back of a hall, even though its strings are thinner than spaghetti.

text: How a Compass Finds North. Deep inside the Earth, a core of hot, liquid iron is constantly churning, and this movement turns the whole planet into a gigantic, weak magnet. Like any magnet, the Earth has two magnetic poles, one near the North Pole and one near the South Pole, and invisible lines of magnetic force loop between them. Scientists call the space around a magnet, where its pull can be felt, a magnetic field. A compass needle is a thin sliver of magnetised metal, balanced on a pin so that it can spin with almost no friction. Because the needle is a tiny magnet itself, its ends are pulled by the Earth's magnetic field, and the needle swings until it lines up with those invisible lines. The end marked in red is attracted towards the magnetic pole in the north, which is why it always settles pointing that way. However, the magnetic pole is not in exactly the same place as the North Pole on a map, and it slowly wanders over the years. Near the far north of Canada, the gap between the two can be so large that a compass is almost useless. That is why a compass and a map can disagree by a few degrees.

frame: Tully gave this speech to the Snowcats the night before the grand final. The Chorrawong was in the front row.
text:
Twelve months ago, we finished last. We lost every game but one, and that one was a draw against a team with eleven players. People laughed at us. Some of you nearly quit. I nearly quit. But Coach Ana told us something I have never forgotten. She said that climbing these peaks isn't about the whole ladder. It's about the next rung. One more rung.

So we trained in the snow. We ran the towers before breakfast, and we ran them again after school. We did push-ups in the hut while Mo cooked dinner, which, if you've tasted his cooking, was the easy part. When our legs were screaming, we said it to each other: one more rung.

In round nine, we were down by thirty points at half-time. Nobody gave up. We clawed back one goal at a time, and we won by a single point. One more rung.

Tomorrow we play the Rams, who haven't lost all year. They're bigger. They're faster. They've won three flags in a row. I'm not going to stand here and promise you we'll win. I'm going to tell you what we'll do. When it hurts, when we're behind, when the crowd goes quiet, we'll take one more rung. And then another.
